key_insight: A prescribed-kinematics Resistive Immersed Surface (RIS) model can reproduce the main hemodynamic behavior of aortic valve flow nearly as well as a fully coupled Immersed Boundary (IB) simulation, but at much lower cost.
engineering_relevance: This suggests RIS is a practical option for valve hemodynamics studies when representative leaflet motion is available and full fluid-structure coupling is not required.
method: Compared RIS in SimVascular svMultiPhysics against fully coupled IB in IBAMR.
Tested both trileaflet and bicuspid aortic valve configurations.
Evaluated bulk flow patterns and transvalvular pressure gradients.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that RIS predicted mean transvalvular pressure gradient within 15% of IB, improving to within 5% when inlet boundary conditions were matched, while cutting computational cost by about 60%.
watch_item: RIS accuracy depends on having realistic prescribed leaflet kinematics and consistent inlet conditions; it is less suitable when leaflet deformation must be solved directly.
paper_title: Comparative analysis of resistive immersed surface and immersed boundary methods for aortic valve simulation
